lede: A data contract is the promise a table makes to everyone who reads it: these columns, these types, these rules. Writing it down as code lets a pipeline check the promise on every load and stop when it's broken.
objectives: Check a table's columns and types against a written contract
Keep data-quality rules as a list of named conditions
Count the rows that fail each rule and put the results in a report DataFrame
Stop a pipeline with an error when a rule fails

blocks.md:
The `claims` table holds insurance claims for clinic visits. Billing, finance and reporting all read it, so they agree on what it contains. A contract has two parts:

- **the shape**: which columns exist and their types;
- **the rules**: what must be true of every row.

The shape comes first, because rules on a missing or mistyped column make no sense. `dtypes` gives every column with its type as text, so a contract can be a plain dict.

blocks.title: Check the shape
blocks.code:
contract = {
    "claim_id": "string",
    "service_date": "date",
    "submitted_date": "date",
    "billed_amount": "decimal(12,2)",
    "allowed_amount": "decimal(12,2)",
    "paid_amount": "double",
    "claim_status": "string",
    "payer_code": "string",
}

actual = dict(claims.dtypes)
for name, wanted in contract.items():
    found = actual.get(name)
    if found != wanted:
        print(f"{name}: expected {wanted}, found {found}")
blocks.note: Two problems: the contract says `paid_amount` is a double but the table stores exact decimals, and `payer_code` doesn't exist (`get` gives `None`). One of them is the contract's mistake, the other the table's. Either way someone has to decide before the data moves on.

blocks.md:
Rules are conditions, so keep them as a list of `(name, condition)` pairs, each **true for a good row**. A Python loop can then check them all the same way.

Decide what a missing value means in each rule. `allowed_amount` is empty until the payer decides, which is fine, so that rule says so with `isNull() |`. As a safety net, `F.coalesce(passes, F.lit(False))` treats any rule that still comes out NULL as a failure, so no row slips through unchecked.

blocks.title: Rules as data, counted in a loop
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

rules = [
    ("dates_in_order", F.col("service_date") <= F.col("submitted_date")),
    ("allowed_within_billed", F.col("allowed_amount").isNull() | (F.col("allowed_amount") <= F.col("billed_amount"))),
    ("known_status", F.col("claim_status").isin("submitted", "approved", "paid", "denied", "appealed")),
]

total = claims.count()
results = []
for name, passes in rules:
    failed = claims.filter(~F.coalesce(passes, F.lit(False))).count()
    results.append((name, failed, total))

report = spark.createDataFrame(results, "rule STRING, failed BIGINT, checked BIGINT")
report.show(truncate=False)
blocks.note: The report is an ordinary DataFrame, built with `createDataFrame` from the Python list. It could be saved next to the data so every load leaves a record of how it scored.

blocks.title: Look at the rows behind a failure
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

dates_in_order = F.col("service_date") <= F.col("submitted_date")

claims.filter(~F.coalesce(dates_in_order, F.lit(False))).select("claim_id", "service_date", "submitted_date", "claim_status").show()
blocks.note: A claim can't be submitted three days before the visit it bills for. A count tells you something is wrong; the rows tell you what.

blocks.md: Some rules depend on another column. Each lab result in `observations` has a code, and each code has exactly one correct unit. A `F.when` chain can work out the expected unit for every row; a code it doesn't know gets NULL, which then fails the rule.

blocks.title: A rule that depends on another column
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

expected_unit = (
    F.when(F.col("code") == "GLU", "mg/dL")
    .when(F.col("code") == "HBA1C", "%")
    .when(F.col("code") == "LDL", "mg/dL")
    .when(F.col("code") == "HGB", "g/dL")
    .when(F.col("code") == "BMI", "kg/m2")
)
unit_ok = F.coalesce(F.col("unit") == expected_unit, F.lit(False))

observations.select("observation_id", "code", "value", "unit", expected_unit.alias("expected_unit"), unit_ok.alias("unit_ok")).show()
blocks.note: Every unit matches here. In a bigger feed this rule catches results sent in the wrong unit, which would otherwise be compared with numbers they don't match.

blocks.md: A report nobody reads doesn't protect anyone. The last step of a contract check is a **gate**: if any rule failed, raise an error so the pipeline stops before the bad data reaches the people who rely on it.

blocks.title: Stop when the contract is broken
blocks.note: The `print` never runs. Raising is deliberate here: the error message names each broken rule and how many rows failed it.

concept.prompt: A rule is `F.col("service_date") <= F.col("submitted_date")` and a claim's `submitted_date` is missing. What does `claims.filter(~F.coalesce(rule, F.lit(False)))` do with that claim?
choices: Leaves it out, because the rule is NULL
Keeps it as a failure, because NULL becomes false
Keeps it only if service_date is also missing
concept.why: The comparison is NULL, `coalesce` turns it into false, and `~` makes it true, so the row is counted as failing.
`dtypes` lists each column with its type as lower-case text, including precision and scale for decimals.

concept.prompt: Why keep rules as a list of `(name, condition)` pairs?
choices: Spark runs a list of rules faster than separate filters
It's the only way to use `F.coalesce`
One loop can check every rule the same way and report each by name
Spark saves the list with the table
concept.why: A condition is an ordinary Python value, so rules can live in a list. Adding a rule is one new line, and the loop counts and names it.

review: A contract is the shape (columns and types) plus the rules every row must follow.
Check the shape first: compare `dict(df.dtypes)` with the types you expect.
Keep rules as `(name, condition)` pairs, each true for a good row, and decide what a missing value means in each.
`F.coalesce(rule, F.lit(False))` makes a NULL rule count as a failure.
Count failures per rule in a loop and build a report with `spark.createDataFrame`.
A gate raises an error when any rule fails, so bad data doesn't move on.
